title: Reds’ Emilio Pagán carted off field after injuring left hamstring on first pitch
content:
CHICAGO — The silence of the visitors’ clubhouse at Wrigley Field after Tuesday night’s 3-2 Cincinnati Reds loss to the Chicago Cubs conveyed the feelings shared by the teammates of closer Emilio Pagán, who was carted off the field in the ninth inning after suffering a left hamstring injury.

“Seeing him go down isn’t good for anybody, especially when you see him come in and see how upset (he was) and tears,” Reds reliever Tony Santillan said. “That does something to somebody when a great person, great human, great teammate, great leader … No one ever wants to see that with anybody.”

Pagán, who blew the save in Monday’s loss, threw just one pitch in the ninth inning Tuesday, grabbing his hamstring immediately after throwing a ball to Cubs leadoff man Nico Hoerner. Pagán hopped around a couple of times before going to the ground, where he was tended to by Reds athletic trainers, and a cart was called to take him off the field.

The 34-year-old Pagán is not only the team’s closer, re-signing with the Reds after his career-best 32 saves in 2025, but he’s also among the most liked and respected members of the team. Even the team’s five-game losing streak and its second walk-off loss in as many nights paled in comparison with the emotions of losing Pagán.

“It’s a tough pill to swallow — as one of our leaders, one of our captains, one of the dudes that cares about this team more than a lot of us,” Reds catcher Jose Trevino said. “He’s a big piece of this. I don’t know the results yet; I’m not a doctor. Obviously, it didn’t look good.”

Reds manager Terry Francona said Pagán would undergo tests on the hamstring Wednesday morning, but he expects Pagán to go on the injured list. Right-hander Pierce Johnson is scheduled to return to the team from bereavement leave Wednesday.

“We’ll know a lot more then,” Francona said. “He’s certainly going to be an IL. We just need to see the extent of how bad he did it, because you could tell by the extent of his reaction that he was struggling.”

Pagán dealt with the same injury last month, but Francona said Pagán told him it hadn’t been bothering him and that he wouldn’t have gone into the game had he felt something while warming up.

It’s been a rough week for the Reds, but especially the bullpen. Over the last seven games, the Reds’ bullpen has had to cover 27 2/3 innings and allowed 31 earned runs. Before the April 29 game against the Colorado Rockies at Great American Ball Park, the Reds bullpen led baseball with a 2.75 ERA. It now stands at 4.21, 16th in all of baseball.

It’s not just been on the field, as two of the team’s relievers, Graham Ashcraft and Johnson, have had stints on the bereavement list in the last week. Trevino has pitched in three games, including multiple innings Saturday in Pittsburgh, where Connor Phillips came into the game in the second inning after starter Rhett Lowder walked the bases loaded. Phillips walked all four batters he faced in that outing, part of an MLB record-tying seven consecutive walked batters.

Aside from Pagán, who was second in the National League in saves in 2025, the Reds have had four other pitchers record saves this season — Santillan, Phillips, Ashcraft and Brock Burke all have one save. Of those four, only Santillan (12) has more than one in his career. Left-hander Sam Moll, Tuesday’s loser, has one career save, and Johnson has 18.

“It’s a big blow to the bullpen, but at the same time, I’ve done it before,” said Santillan, who gave up a game-tying homer to the Cubs’ Michael Busch in the eighth inning. “We’ve got the guys back there. We’re obviously on a little bit of a skid here, but everyone believes in each other.”

The Reds left Great American Ball Park on Thursday in first place in the NL Central and will not be when they return Friday to begin a series with the Houston Astros. The Reds are in third place in the division, four games behind the Cubs and 1.5 games behind the St. Louis Cardinals.

When asked whether the Reds were “snakebit,” Trevino bristled.

“I don’t know if I’m going to use the word ‘snakebit,’” Trevino said. “I’ll use the word ‘baseball’ — things are going to happen, baseball is unpredictable. Things like this are going to happen, so it’s up to our team to keep playing.”
